title: Case study: video streaming (YouTube / Netflix)

kcs.statement: An uploaded video is split into chunks and transcoded in parallel by workers into several resolutions and codecs. A pipeline of queued tasks marks the video ready when every rendition finishes.
With adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH), each rendition is cut into segments a few seconds long and listed in a manifest. The player picks the bitrate for each segment from the measured bandwidth.
Video egress dominates cost. Popular videos are served from CDN edge servers, and long-tail videos may be served from origin or regional caches.
Storage per uploaded minute is multiplied by the number of renditions. Five resolutions can store about 2-3× the bytes of the original.

problem_ideas: 500 hours uploaded per minute at 1 GB/hour across 5 renditions: compute daily storage.
10M concurrent viewers at an average of 3 Mbps: compute peak egress in Tbps.
A viewer's bandwidth drops from 8 to 2 Mbps. Predict what the player does at the next segment.
Choose push or pull CDN for a Netflix-style catalogue and for user uploads.
Transcoding one chunk fails. Design a retry without redoing the whole video.
Estimate how 2-second and 10-second segments change startup latency and request rate.
